sections.title: Link the story to their pain

items.q: How do you turn a personal story into client-relevant advice?
items.a: Ask *"What does this story symbolize?"* while listening, then bridge to their problem (**story-symbolize-link**). Louise linked hunger/foot pain → client's **back pain** → *don't treat loved ones with a thong slap*, then closed with **"The reason I'm telling you this…"**

items.q: Why should stories include dialogue and character voices?
items.a: **Back-and-forth lines** and distinct voices pull listeners into the scene. Peak action needs spoken exchange — Louise got coached to play **both voices** before the flip-flop throw; Greg used Master Ting's *"just do the technique and shut up."*

items.q: What kind of detail makes a character land?
items.a: **Specificity**: names and sensory detail beat generics. **Master Ting** vs "my teacher"; **sore feet, hiking, hunger, flip-flops** paint pictures a summary cannot.

items.q: How should you structure a story for impact?
items.a: Cut the boring bits — Spielberg via Vinh: *"A movie is just **life without the boring bits**."* Build around one **peak emotional or action moment** (engagement argument, forest "stream" reveal).

items.q: What is the difference between reliving and reporting a story?
items.a: **Relive, don't report**: act out the moment (look over shoulder, chuckle, feel it) instead of listing historical facts. When **you feel it, the audience feels it**.

items.q: How playful should you be when telling stories?
items.a: Dial playfulness up — Vinh asked Louise to take it from **2 → 8**. Over-animate, exaggerate, use a "dopey guy voice"; you're **playing a character**, not performing as yourself in a safe room.

items.q: Why workshop a story twice instead of waiting for perfection?
items.a: **Test and iterate**: redo immediately after coaching. Round one → round two is the process. **Inspiration comes from taking action**, not hoarding knowledge — start anywhere; permission to begin beats waiting for the perfect story.
